summary: AstraSight is our entry for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". On long missions such as a trip to Mars, a doctor on Earth can be up to 22 minutes away, one way, so astronauts have to watch their own health. Our answer is a spacesuit helmet with a health display inside the visor and ASTRA, an AI assistant that works in the helmet and on the ship. ASTRA shows eight vital signs in green, amber and red, explains them in plain words, suggests what to do, and lets the flight surgeon know when a problem is serious. The website includes a live helmet HUD, an EVA screen with solar-flare warnings, a suit check that blocks unsafe suits, and a medical bay with a clickable body map. ASTRA runs on local AI models (Qwen 2.5 and MedGemma), so it keeps working without a link to Earth, and it can show real readings from a Garmin watch. All other health data is simulated: AstraSight is a concept prototype, not a medical device. Next, we would like to add smart handrails that measure grip, pulse and stress every time a crew member grabs one.
details:
What it does and how it works

AstraSight is a concept for a spacesuit helmet with a health display inside the visor, together with ASTRA (Astronaut Support, Triage & Response Assistant), an AI assistant that works in the helmet and on the ship. Crew sign in with a face scan, and ASTRA asks a few questions to learn what's normal for each person. From then on, the visor shows eight indicators: heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing, a pupil scan, cognitive load, core temperature, radiation dose and stress (HRV). Each one is colored green, amber or red. Astronauts can talk to ASTRA or type to her. She explains readings in plain words, gives step-by-step advice, and sends serious findings to the flight surgeon. The site also includes:

an EVA screen with a solar-flare shelter countdown

a suit check that marks a suit NO-GO when a life-support sensor fails, and offers a spare suit

a medical bay with a clickable body map, where a medical AI suggests what to check next

a crew-wide view for the Crew Medical Officer

guided ultrasound

"send to flight surgeon", with the real signal delay for the ISS, the Moon or Mars

Benefits

Astronauts can check their health at a glance, without medical training and without using their hands. ASTRA runs on local AI models, so she keeps working when the link to Earth is slow or down. She catches problems early, both in the body and in the equipment: she doesn't trust a suit sensor that gives impossible readings.

Intended impact

On long missions, crews have to be more self-reliant. We want astronauts to notice warning signs early, act on them, and know when to ask for help. That makes the crew safer and helps flight surgeons focus on the cases that need them. The same idea could help people in other isolated places, such as Antarctic stations, ships or remote areas.

Tools and technologies

Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step. three.js for the 3D helmet, Tailwind CSS on the report screen.

Backend: Node.js with no extra packages.

AI:

Qwen 2.5 and MedGemma 1.5, running locally through Ollama

Gemini Flash for the first-visit questionnaire

ElevenLabs for ASTRA's voice

the Web Speech API for voice input

Sign-in: face-api.js for face recognition, Firebase Authentication.

Hardware: a Garmin Forerunner 255 running our own Connect IQ app (written in Monkey C), plus Bluetooth heart-rate input.

Testing and media: Playwright for testing. Python for the promo video and its music.

Hosting: Oracle Cloud with a Cloudflare Tunnel.

AI coding help: we used Claude Code (Anthropic) as a coding assistant during development.

What makes it creative

The helmet has no buttons, because a pressurized glove can't press them. You look to select and talk to command.

ASTRA is a pixel-art character who changes outfits for her role: an engineer for suit checks, a doctor in the medical bay.

She checks the sensors as well as the readings, so a broken sensor can't hide a real problem.

The site follows real mission situations, from a solar flare during a spacewalk to a crew-wide health pattern spotted in the medical bay.

Factors we considered

NASA's five spaceflight hazards (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity and the closed environment), and the delay in reaching Earth.

Users without medical training: plain language, color coding at a glance, and step-by-step instructions.

Safety: ASTRA flags problems and suggests actions, but never diagnoses, and serious findings always go to the flight surgeon.

Privacy: only face descriptors (128 numbers per face) are stored, never photos, and crew see only their own record.

Roles: crew members and the Crew Medical Officer have different needs.

Honesty: all health data is simulated except the Garmin watch readings. AstraSight is a concept prototype, not a medical device.
